title: Unique normalized strict-system first slot shift
statement: Fix a prime l, a finite extension E of Q_l, an arbitrary scheme W and an integer r. There exists exactly one natural isomorphism moving the shift r in the strict-system first slot to a shift of the tensor output, satisfying systemTensorLeftProperty of [def-pur-integral-tensor-shift-properties]. The normalization is required on every resolving pair, with no condition that l be invertible on W. Uniqueness is equality of the natural isomorphisms, not merely existence of an isomorphism between their endpoints.

proof.text: Use the unsigned Mathlib mapBifunctorShift₁Iso on the actual coefficient-module total tensor. Its summand formula, applied to the sheafified pure tensor, gives systemTensorLeftFormula. Its naturality in both factors gives the natural cochain comparison. Shifting preserves K-flatness: tensoring an acyclic complex with the shifted second factor is isomorphic to the shift of the original acyclic tensor. The natural comparison is the generic tensorFirstShiftIso from the existing slice-tensor integer-shift proof; its component is identified with mapBifunctorShift₁Iso.

The K-flat inclusion followed by Q is a localization at quasi-isomorphisms, by the proved kFlatLocalization helper of the ringed-derived tensor-Hom adjunction. On pairs of K-flat complexes conjugate the cochain comparison by the tensor-model comparison and Q.commShiftIso. Localize this natural isomorphism along the product localization. The component formula for liftNatTrans proves the required normalization on every K-flat pair.

Two normalized comparisons agree on every pure tensor, hence their cochain maps agree: use total-coproduct extensionality, the sheafification adjunction and tensor-product extensionality on sections. Cancel the input shift comparison in the representative normalization to identify their derived components on every K-flat pair. Each derived object has a K-flat representative by the K-flat resolution theorem; naturality along the representative isomorphisms then identifies every component, proving equality of the natural isomorphisms.
